title: One Word Substitution
summary: A phrase such as 'murder of a king' must be replaced by one word (regicide). Options are built from suffix families —cide, -phobia, -logy, -cracy, -phile — so classifying the family first kills half the options. The bank below carries 150+ exam-frequency substitutions grouped for daily revision.

subtopics.title: Suffix families: decode the word by its ending
subtopics.concept:
One-word-substitution items rarely need a giant dictionary — the ending of the answer already tells you its *family*, and options are built one per family. Learn the suffix, and every member of the family is within reach.

**-cide — the act of killing**

• Regicide – killing a king
• Genocide – killing a whole race or community
• Fratricide – killing one's own brother
• Infanticide – killing an infant
• Patricide – killing one's father
• Suicide – killing oneself
• Homicide – killing a human being
• Sororicide – killing one's sister

**-phobia — an abnormal fear of**

• Hydrophobia – fear of water
• Claustrophobia – fear of confined spaces
• Acrophobia – fear of heights
• Xenophobia – fear or dislike of foreigners
• Nyctophobia – fear of darkness
• Haematophobia – fear of blood
• Triskaidekaphobia – fear of the number thirteen
• Photophobia – abnormal sensitivity to light

**-ology — the study of**

• Anthropology – study of humankind's development
• Ornithology – study of birds
• Entomology – study of insects
• Zoology – study of animals
• Philology – study of languages and their history
• Etymology – study of word origins
• Geology – study of the earth's rocks
• Psychology – study of the mind
• Sociology – study of society
• Seismology – study of earthquakes

**-graphy / -grapher — writing/recording, or its practitioner**

• Geography – study of the earth's surface
• Demography – statistical study of populations
• Calligraphy – the art of fine handwriting
• Cartography – the making of maps
• Hagiography – writing of saints' lives
• Lexicographer – one who compiles dictionaries

**-cracy / -crat — rule or power**

• Democracy – government by the people
• Autocracy – rule by one absolute ruler
• Bureaucracy – government by paid officials
• Aristocracy – rule by the noble class
• Theocracy – rule in the name of God
• Plutocracy – rule by the wealthy
• Mobocracy – rule by the mob
• Meritocracy – rule by ability and merit

**-phile / -phile words — one who loves**

• Bibliophile – a lover of books
• Philatelist – a lover and collector of stamps
• Anglophile – a lover of England or English ways
• Philanthropist – one who loves humankind through charity

**-vore / -phagous — feeding on**

• Carnivorous – flesh-eating
• Herbivorous – plant-eating
• Insectivorous – insect-eating
• Omnivorous – eating everything

**-gamy / -gamy words — marriage patterns**

• Monogamy – marriage to one person at a time
• Polygamy – marriage to several spouses
• Bigamy – marrying while legally married to another
• Exogamy – marriage outside one's own group

**How the family method wins.** The stem 'murder of a king' invites four options, usually one -cide word, one -ology word, one -phobia word, one person-word. Knowing -cide = killing filters to the candidates, and then plain sense (rex = king → regicide) finishes. You never needed to memorise 'regicide' as a whole.

**Stack two families for rare words.** *Nyctophobia* = nycto (night) + phobia (fear) → fear of darkness. *Entomology* = entomo (insect) + logy (study). Rare SSC words are nearly always transparent stacks — the examiner picks words that reward this decoding.

**TheGreek/Latin counting prefixes** multiply coverage: mono (one), bi/duo (two), tri (three), quad (four), poly (many), pan (all), omni (all), semi (half), hemi (half), cent (hundred), milli (thousand). *Omnipotent/omniscient/omnipresent* are one prefix + one root each.

tricks.title: Family filter
tricks.body: Classify the stem first: is it a killing word, a fear, a study, a ruler-system, a person-type, a place? Reject every option from a different family before reading further.

example.q: Murder of a king: homicide / regicide / ornithology / hydrophobia.
example.solution: Killing stem → -cide family only → regicide (rex/reg = king). Homicide kills 'a human' generally — the specific stem wins.

tricks.title: Root + suffix stack
tricks.body: Split rare answers: nycto-phobia, entomo-logy, carto-grapher. Two known parts beat one memorised word.

tricks.title: Counting-prefix drill
tricks.body: One evening per prefix set: mono-, bi-, tri-, poly-, pan-, omni-. Write each with three familiar words and the family stays for life.

mistakes: Confusing fratricide (brother) with patricide (father) — the family root carries the relation.
Mixing -phobia (fear) with -phile (love) under exam pressure.
Choosing astrology for a 'scientific study of stars' stem — astronomy is the science, astrology the belief system.
Memorising isolated words instead of suffix families; the family is what survives pressure.
subtopics.notes:
### What one-word substitution means
In this question you get a group of words, such as *the killing of a king*, and you choose the single word that means the same thing: **regicide**. The exam checks whether you know the word and whether you can separate it from words that look similar.

The good news: most answer words are made of **two parts** — a root (the object) and a suffix (the family). If you know the parts, you can build the meaning even for a word you have never seen.

### The main families
| Suffix | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| -cide | killing | regicide (king), fratricide (brother), patricide (father), matricide (mother), infanticide (infant), genocide (a whole race), homicide (a human), suicide (oneself) |
| -phobia | abnormal fear | hydrophobia (water), acrophobia (heights), claustrophobia (closed spaces), xenophobia (foreigners), nyctophobia (darkness) |
| -logy | study of | ornithology (birds), entomology (insects), seismology (earthquakes), etymology (word origins), anthropology (humankind) |
| -graphy / -grapher | writing, drawing | cartography (map-making), calligraphy (beautiful handwriting), lexicographer (dictionary maker) |
| -phile / phil- | lover of | bibliophile (books), philatelist (stamps), philanthropist (lover of mankind, gives to charity) |
| -vore / -vorous | eater of | herbivore (plants), carnivore (flesh), omnivore (both), insectivore (insects) |
| -gamy | marriage | monogamy (one spouse), polygamy (more than one spouse at a time), misogamy (hatred of marriage) |

### Roots worth knowing
- **reg** = king, **frater** = brother, **pater** = father, **mater** = mother, **geno** = race.
- **hydro** = water, **acro** = height, **xeno** = foreign, **nycto** = night.
- **ornitho** = bird, **entomo** = insect, **seismo** = earthquake, **etymo** = true meaning of a word.
- **biblio** = book, **herb** = plant, **carn** = flesh, **omni** = all, **poly** = many, **mono** = one.

Worked example: *nyctophobia* = nycto (night) + phobia (fear) → fear of darkness. You did not need to memorise it as one word.

### How the options are built
A typical question has one right word and three words from the **same or a nearby family**. For *study of insects*, you may see entomology, etymology, ornithology and seismology — all -logy words. So the family step removes nothing here; the **root** decides. Always check both parts.

In other questions the options come from different families: *fear of heights* with acrophobia, acrobat, acronym, acropolis. Here the family step (-phobia = fear) alone finds the answer.

### Look-alike traps
- **entomology** (insects) vs **etymology** (word origins) — one letter group apart.
- **patricide** (father) vs **fratricide** (brother) vs **matricide** (mother).
- **philatelist** (stamps) vs **numismatist** (coins).
- **-phobia** (fear) vs **-phile** (love).
- **astronomy** (science of stars) vs **astrology** (predicting the future from stars).

### Quick revision
| Suffix | Family |
|---|---|
| -cide | killing |
| -phobia | fear |
| -logy | study |
| -graphy / -grapher | writing, drawing, recording |
| -phile | lover |
| -vore | eater |
| -gamy | marriage |

- Split the word: root + suffix.
- Family first, then root.
- Card the look-alike pairs: entomology/etymology, patricide/fratricide, philatelist/numismatist.

patterns.name: Killing words (-cide)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem says 'killing of ...' or 'murder of ...' and names a victim (king, brother, father, mother, infant, race).
patterns.logic:
1. Confirm the family: killing → -cide.
2. Match the victim to its root: reg = king, frater = brother, pater = father, mater = mother, geno = race.
3. Choose the word with that root; reject the general 'homicide' if a specific victim is named.

*Why it works:* every -cide word is victim-root + cide, so the victim decides.

example.q: *The killing of an infant* — (a) infanticide (b) genocide (c) regicide (d) suicide
example.solution: Victim = infant → **(a) infanticide**.

patterns.name: Fear words (-phobia)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem says 'an abnormal fear of ...'.
patterns.logic:
1. Family: fear → -phobia.
2. Match the feared thing to its root: hydro = water, acro = height, claustro = closed place, xeno = foreigner, nycto = night.
3. Reject look-alike non-phobia words (acrobat, hydrant).

*Why it works:* the root names the fear; the suffix only says it is a fear.

example.q: *An abnormal fear of darkness* — (a) nyctophobia (b) hydrophobia (c) acrophobia (d) claustrophobia
example.solution: nycto = night → **(a) nyctophobia**.

patterns.name: Study words (-logy)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem says 'the study of ...' or 'the science of ...'.
patterns.logic:
1. Family: study → -logy.
2. Match the subject: birds → ornithology, insects → entomology, earthquakes → seismology, word origins → etymology.
3. Watch the entomology/etymology trap.

*Why it works:* all options are usually -logy words, so only the root separates them.

example.q: *The study of mankind, its origins and cultures* — (a) anthropology (b) ornithology (c) entomology (d) etymology
example.solution: anthropo = human → **(a) anthropology**.

patterns.name: Lover, eater and marriage words (-phile, -vore, -gamy)
patterns.howToSpot: The stem says 'a lover/collector of ...', 'an animal that feeds on ...', or describes a marriage practice.
patterns.logic:
1. Pick the family: love → phil-, eat → -vore, marriage → -gamy.
2. Match the root: biblio = books, herb = plants, carn = flesh, mono = one, poly = many.
3. Reject the look-alike (philatelist vs numismatist; monogamy vs polygamy).

*Why it works:* the same two-part logic applies to every family.

example.q: *An animal that eats both plants and flesh* — (a) omnivore (b) herbivore (c) carnivore (d) insectivore
example.solution: omni = all → **(a) omnivore**.

subtopics.title: One word for people: traits, trades and types
subtopics.concept:
The largest OWS category names a *person by what they do, feel or suffer*. Four sub-buckets organise the bank:

**1. Trades and professions** (learn with the tool or object of the trade): cobbler–shoes, plumber–pipes, cartographer–maps, lexicographer–dictionaries, obstetrician–childbirth, astronomer–stars (science), astrologer–stars (prediction).

**2. Character and conduct:** miser (hoards money), spendthrift (wastes it), teetotaller (never drinks), glutton (overeats), garrulous (overtalkative), taciturn (speaks little), gullible (believes easily), sceptic (doubts), novice (beginner), veteran (long-experienced).

**3. Loyalty and betrayal:** patriot/traitor, martyr (dies for a cause), apostate (abandons his religion), vandal (destroys property for pleasure), firebrand (stirs up unrest).

**4. Omnipotence set:** omnipotent (all-powerful), omniscient (all-knowing), omnipresent (present everywhere) — three words, one prefix, endlessly reused.

**People bank (revise in five-word batches)**

| One-word substitution | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **One who talks in sleep** | Somniloquist |
| **One who walks in sleep** | Somnambulist |
| **One who cannot read or write** | Illiterate |
| **One who knows many languages** | Polyglot |
| **One who lives shut off from the world** | Recluse (or Hermit) |
| **One who spends beyond his means to impress** | Extravagant (a spendthrift) |
| **One who is extremely careful with money** | Miser |
| **One who never drinks alcohol** | Teetotaller |
| **One who deals in cattle** | Drover |
| **One who mends shoes** | Cobbler |
| **One who cuts and sells men's clothing** | Tailor (a men's outfitter) |
| **One who sells medicines and prepares them** | Pharmacist (or Chemist) |
| **One who performs surgical operations** | Surgeon |
| **One who fits and repairs water pipes** | Plumber |
| **One who makes maps** | Cartographer |
| **One who compiles a dictionary** | Lexicographer |
| **One who writes the life history of another** | Biographer |
| **One who writes his own life story** | Autobiographer |
| **One who studies the human mind** | Psychologist |
| **One who treats eye disorders** | Oculist (or Optometrist) |
| **One who treats teeth** | Dentist |
| **One who foretells events by the stars** | Astrologer |
| **One who studies the stars scientifically** | Astronomer |
| **One who travels in space** | Astronaut (or Cosmonaut) |
| **One who is new to a profession** | Novice (or Tyro) |
| **One who has long experience of a field** | Veteran |
| **A person appointed to hear and decide a dispute** | Arbitrator |
| **One who deliberately damages property** | Vandal |
| **One who incites others to violence** | Firebrand |
| **A person who loves his country deeply** | Patriot |
| **One who betrays his country** | Traitor |
| **A person of great courage** | Valiant (a gallant) |
| **One unable to speak** | Dumb (speech-impaired) |
| **One unable to hear** | Deaf |
| **One who is present everywhere** | Omnipresent |
| **One who knows everything** | Omniscient |
| **One with unlimited power** | Omnipotent |
| **A woman whose husband has died** | Widow |
| **A man whose wife has died** | Widower |
| **One who has just been married** | Newly-wed (bride/groom) |
| **One who eats too much** | Glutton |
| **One who talks too much** | Garrulous (or Loquacious) |
| **One who speaks little** | Taciturn (or Reserved) |
| **One who believes everything easily** | Gullible |
| **One who doubts everything** | Sceptic |
| **One who hates humankind** | Misanthrope |
| **One who sacrifices life for a cause** | Martyr |
| **One who deserts his religion** | Apostate |
| **One who avoids company and merriment** | Introvert (a recluse) |
| **One who shows off his learning** | Pedant |

**Sensory and status pairs** are quick marks: dumb/speech-impaired, deaf, widow/widower, newly-wed. Note the gender-symmetric pairs — SSC loves the widow/widower switch under time pressure.

tricks.title: Object-anchor the trade
tricks.body: Never learn 'cobbler' alone — learn 'cobbler → shoes'. Stems name the object ('one who repairs shoes'), and your anchor matches it instantly.

tricks.title: Contrast pairs together
tricks.body: Store opposites and neighbours in one card: garrulous ↔ taciturn; miser ↔ spendthrift; novice ↔ veteran. The stem often points to one side of a pair.

tricks.title: Omni-triplet
tricks.body: One prefix (omni- = all), three endings: -potent (power), -scient (knowing), -present (place). One card covers all three SSC favourites.

mistakes: Swapping astrologer and astronomer — decide by 'scientific' or 'prediction' in the stem.
Using 'mediator' where the stem demands an authorised decider — arbitrator decides, a mediator facilitates.
Mixing spendthrift (wastes) with miser (hoards).
Answering with an adjective when the stem's pattern expects the person-word.
subtopics.notes:
### The biggest group: words for people
The most common one-word-substitution stem begins with **'One who ...'** or **'A person who ...'**. These words name a person by their job, habit, feeling or situation.

### Four boxes to sort people words
**1. Jobs (trades and professions).** Learn each with the object of the job.
| Word | Job |
|---|---|
| cartographer | makes maps |
| lexicographer | writes dictionaries |
| cobbler | mends shoes |
| plumber | fits and repairs water pipes |
| paediatrician | doctor for children |
| dermatologist | doctor for the skin |
| astronomer | studies stars scientifically |
| astrologer | predicts the future from stars |

**2. Habits and character.**
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| teetotaller | never drinks alcohol |
| glutton | eats too much |
| miser | hoards money and hates spending |
| spendthrift | wastes money |
| gullible | easily deceived |
| sceptic | doubts everything |
| garrulous | talks too much |
| taciturn | speaks very little |

**3. Pairs and opposites.** Examiners love to put the partner word as a wrong option.
- widow (woman whose husband has died) / widower (man whose wife has died)
- novice (beginner) / veteran (very experienced)
- miser / spendthrift
- optimist (hopes for the best) / pessimist (expects the worst)

**4. Words built from roots.**
| Word | Parts | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| polyglot | poly (many) + glot (tongue) | knows many languages |
| misanthrope | mis (hate) + anthrope (man) | hates mankind |
| philanthropist | phil (love) + anthrop (man) | loves mankind, gives to charity |
| misogynist | mis (hate) + gyn (woman) | hates women |
| somnambulist | somn (sleep) + ambul (walk) | walks in sleep |
| omniscient | omni (all) + scient (knowing) | knows everything |

### Worked examples
*One who studies the stars scientifically* → the word 'scientifically' decides → **astronomer**, not astrologer.

*A man whose wife has died* → **widower**. 'Widow' is the partner word planted as a trap.

*One who knows many languages* → poly = many → **polyglot**. 'Polymath' (knows many subjects) is the look-alike.

### How to answer
1. Underline the key detail: the object (maps, children, shoes), the habit (drinks, talks, spends), or the gender.
2. Put the stem into its box: job, habit, pair or root-word.
3. Choose the option that matches the detail exactly. Reject the partner word and the look-alike.

### Quick revision
- Learn job words with their object: cartographer–maps, lexicographer–dictionary, paediatrician–children.
- Habit words come in opposite pairs: miser/spendthrift, garrulous/taciturn, gullible/sceptic.
- Gender pairs: widow/widower.
- Roots: poly (many), mis (hate), phil (love), omni (all), somn (sleep).

patterns.name: Person by job or profession
patterns.howToSpot: Stem: 'One who makes/repairs/treats/studies ...' naming an object or a field.
patterns.logic:
1. Underline the object (maps, dictionaries, children, skin).
2. Recall the job word linked to that object.
3. Reject words from nearby jobs (cartographer vs calligrapher).

*Why it works:* job words are defined by their object, so the object decides.

example.q: *A doctor who treats skin diseases* — (a) dermatologist (b) paediatrician (c) cardiologist (d) neurologist
example.solution: derma = skin → **(a) dermatologist**.

patterns.name: Person by habit or character
patterns.howToSpot: Stem describes a habit or nature: never drinks, overeats, easily fooled, talks too much.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the habit in one word (drinking, eating, trusting, talking).
2. Recall the pair of words on that habit (glutton/abstemious, garrulous/taciturn).
3. Pick the side the stem describes.

*Why it works:* options often include the opposite habit word as a trap.

example.q: *One who speaks very little* — (a) taciturn (b) garrulous (c) eloquent (d) loquacious
example.solution: Speaks little → **(a) taciturn**. Garrulous and loquacious mean the opposite.

patterns.name: Partner-word trap (gender or opposite pairs)
patterns.howToSpot: The options contain both members of a pair: widow/widower, miser/spendthrift, novice/veteran.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the deciding detail (man or woman? saves or wastes? new or old?).
2. Choose the member of the pair that matches it.
3. Do not pick the familiar-looking partner.

*Why it works:* the examiner adds the partner so a hurried reader picks it.

example.q: *One who has long experience in a field* — (a) veteran (b) novice (c) amateur (d) apprentice
example.solution: Long experience → **(a) veteran**. Novice is the opposite partner.

patterns.name: Root-built person words
patterns.howToSpot: The answer is a Greek or Latin-built word: poly-, mis-, phil-, omni-, somn-.
patterns.logic:
1. Split each option into prefix + root.
2. Match the parts to the stem (many + tongue = many languages).
3. Reject the option with a similar prefix but a different root.

*Why it works:* rare person words are almost always transparent root stacks.

example.q: *One who walks in sleep* — (a) somnambulist (b) somniloquist (c) insomniac (d) pedestrian
example.solution: somn (sleep) + ambul (walk) → **(a) somnambulist**. Somniloquist talks in sleep.

subtopics.title: One word for places and groups
subtopics.concept:
**Places.** The stem pattern is 'a place where X is kept/stored/done'. Anchor each place to its stored object:

**Places bank**

| One-word substitution | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A place where bees are kept** | Apiary |
| **A place where birds are kept** | Aviary |
| **A place where fish are kept** | Aquarium |
| **A place where grains are stored** | Granary |
| **A place where horses are kept** | Stable |
| **A place where money is coined** | Mint |
| **A place where weapons are stored** | Armoury |
| **A place where dead bodies are kept** | Mortuary |
| **A place where orphans live** | Orphanage |
| **A place where historical objects are displayed** | Museum |
| **A place where aircraft are kept and repaired** | Hangar |
| **A place where novels, poems etc. are produced** | Publishing house (or Press) |
| **A place for public speaking and debate** | Podium (the speaker's platform) |
| **A burial place outside a church** | Cemetery |
| **A place where monks live together** | Monastery |
| **A place where nuns live together** | Convent |
| **A building where goods are made by hand or machine** | Factory (or Workshop) |
| **A place where animals are slaughtered** | Abattoir |

Watch the near-pairs: *apiary* (bees) vs *aviary* (birds) differ by one letter; *granary* (grain) vs *granite* (rock) — the exam plants exactly these neighbours as options.

**Groups (collective nouns).** The stem pattern is 'a group of X':

**Groups bank**

| One-word substitution | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A group of lions** | Pride |
| **A group of wolves** | Pack |
| **A group of bees** | Swarm |
| **A group of sheep** | Flock |
| **A group of cattle** | Herd |
| **A group of fish** | School (or Shoal) |
| **A group of stars forming a pattern** | Constellation |
| **A group of islands** | Archipelago |
| **A group of skilled judges or experts** | Panel |
| **A group of worshippers** | Congregation |
| **A group of musicians playing together** | Orchestra (or Band) |
| **A group of soldiers** | Troop (or Platoon) |
| **A group of ships sailing together** | Fleet |
| **A group of hairs growing together** | Tuft |

Collective nouns are pure memorisation but tiny in number — twenty cover nearly every paper. Note the precision points: lions come in a *pride* (not a herd), wolves in a *pack*, fish in a *school*, islands in an *archipelago* (not a chain of villages!).

**Choosing between group options** is a one-letter game under pressure: swarm (bees/insects), flock (sheep/birds), herd (cattle), pride (lions), pack (wolves/dogs). Ask which animal the stem names before touching the options.

tricks.title: Stored-object anchor
tricks.body: Places are defined by what is inside: bees→apiary, birds→aviary, grain→granary, coins→mint, corpses→mortuary. Match the object, not the sound.

example.q: A place where bees are kept: aviary / apiary / aquarium / granary.
example.solution: Bees → **apiary**. 'Aviary' differs by one letter — the deliberate neighbour-trap.

tricks.title: Animal-first matching
tricks.body: For group stems, name the animal first, then recall its partner noun. Options scramble the five common pairs; the animal decides.

tricks.title: Near-pair cards
tricks.body: Make cards for one-letter pairs: apiary/aviary, granary/granite, monastery/convent (men/women). These are where marks leak.

mistakes: Choosing 'aviary' for bees (one-letter trap).
Calling a lion group a 'herd' — lions take 'pride'.
Confusing monastery (men) and convent (women).
Using 'army' for a group of soldiers in the collective-noun sense when the stem wants 'troop/platoon'.
subtopics.notes:
### Two simple question shapes
1. **'A place where ___ is kept / done'** → a place word.
2. **'A group of ___'** → a collective noun.
Both are pure matching: the stem names the thing, you name its place or group.

### Places: match the thing kept inside
| Place | What is kept or done there |
|---|---|
| apiary | bees |
| aviary | birds |
| aquarium | fish and water animals |
| granary | grain |
| armoury / arsenal | weapons |
| mint | coins are made |
| hangar | aircraft are kept and repaired |
| kennel | dogs |
| stable | horses |
| mortuary | dead bodies (before burial or post-mortem) |
| cemetery | burial ground |
| abattoir | animals are killed for meat |
| monastery | monks live |
| convent | nuns live |
| orphanage | orphans live |
| observatory | stars are studied through telescopes |

Worked example: *A place where coins are made* → **mint**. A treasury keeps money but does not make coins, so it is wrong.

### One-letter and look-alike traps
- **apiary** (bees) vs **aviary** (birds). Remember: *api* sounds like 'ape-bee'; *avi* as in aviation (flying birds).
- **monastery** (monks, men) vs **convent** (nuns, women).
- **mortuary** (bodies kept) vs **cemetery** (bodies buried).
- **hangar** (aircraft) vs **hanger** (for clothes) — spelling matters.

### Groups: the collective nouns
| Group of | Word |
|---|---|
| lions | pride |
| wolves, dogs | pack |
| cattle | herd |
| sheep, birds | flock |
| bees | swarm |
| fish | school / shoal |
| ships | fleet |
| islands | archipelago |
| stars in a pattern | constellation |
| flowers | bouquet |
| worshippers in a church | congregation |
| musicians | orchestra / band |

Worked example: *A group of wolves* → **pack**. Lions take pride, cattle take herd — the animal decides.

### How to answer
1. Find the key noun in the stem (bees, coins, wolves, islands).
2. Recall its partner place or group word.
3. Check the look-alike trap before you mark.

These questions are fast marks. Twenty place words and twenty group words cover almost every paper, so learn them in one sitting and revise weekly. While revising, always say the partner word aloud — *bees–apiary, coins–mint, wolves–pack, islands–archipelago* — because the exam never asks for a definition, only for the partner.

### Quick revision
- Places: apiary (bees), aviary (birds), granary (grain), mint (coins), hangar (aircraft), mortuary (bodies), abattoir (slaughter), monastery (monks), convent (nuns).
- Groups: pride (lions), pack (wolves), herd (cattle), flock (sheep), swarm (bees), fleet (ships), archipelago (islands), constellation (stars).
- Traps: apiary/aviary, monastery/convent, mortuary/cemetery.

patterns.name: Place where something is kept or made
patterns.howToSpot: Stem: 'A place where ___ are kept / stored / made'.
patterns.logic:
1. Underline the thing kept (bees, grain, coins, aircraft).
2. Recall the place word for that thing.
3. Check one-letter look-alikes (apiary/aviary).

*Why it works:* each place word is tied to one stored thing.

example.q: *A place where dogs are kept* — (a) kennel (b) stable (c) aviary (d) apiary
example.solution: Dogs → **(a) kennel**. Stable is for horses.

patterns.name: Place named by the people or activity in it
patterns.howToSpot: Stem: 'A place where monks live', 'where bodies are kept', 'where animals are slaughtered'.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify who lives there or what happens there.
2. Match: monks → monastery, nuns → convent, bodies → mortuary, slaughter → abattoir.
3. Separate close pairs (mortuary vs cemetery).

*Why it works:* the activity or resident fixes one word.

example.q: *A place where nuns live* — (a) convent (b) monastery (c) seminary (d) orphanage
example.solution: Nuns → **(a) convent**. Monastery is for monks.

patterns.name: Collective noun for animals
patterns.howToSpot: Stem: 'A group of lions / wolves / cattle / bees / sheep'.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the animal.
2. Recall its partner: pride, pack, herd, swarm, flock.
3. Do not be swayed by options that fit other animals.

*Why it works:* the options are the same five words shuffled; the animal decides.

example.q: *A group of sheep* — (a) flock (b) pride (c) pack (d) swarm
example.solution: Sheep → **(a) flock**.

patterns.name: Collective noun for things or people
patterns.howToSpot: Stem: 'A group of islands / stars / ships / flowers / worshippers'.
patterns.logic:
1. Name the thing grouped.
2. Recall the partner word: archipelago, constellation, fleet, bouquet, congregation.
3. Reject geography or science words that are not groups (peninsula, comet).

*Why it works:* each group word belongs to one kind of thing.

example.q: *A bunch of flowers* — (a) bouquet (b) cluster (c) bundle (d) heap
example.solution: Flowers → **(a) bouquet**.

subtopics.title: Government systems, studies and word-craft
subtopics.concept:
**Government by whom?** The stem always names the ruler — match the ruler to the suffix -cracy or the classical root:

- by the **people** → democracy; by **officials** → bureaucracy; by the **rich** → plutocracy; by the **nobles** → aristocracy; by **God/clergy** → theocracy; by **one** → autocracy/dictatorship; by **the mob** → mobocracy (or ochlocracy); **no government** → anarchy; **rule by a king/queen** → monarchy.

**Studies and -graphy words:** geography (earth's surface), demography (populations), cartography (maps), calligraphy (beautiful writing), hagiography (saints' lives), etymology (word origins), philology (language history). The stem 'study of ___' names the object; the -ology/-graphy suffix names the family.

**Speech and writing words** form their own tight set — prologue/epilogue (start/end of a literary work), epitaph (tomb inscription), elegy (mourning poem), eulogy (words of praise for the dead), euphemism (mild substitute for a harsh word), soliloquy (talking to oneself), extempore (unprepared). Two overlapping pairs are the classic traps: *elegy vs eulogy* (both about the dead: mourning vs praise) and *epitaph vs epilogue* (tomb vs play's end).

**Time and frequency words:** century (100 years), decade (10), annual (yearly), biennial (every two years), biannual (twice a year), diurnal (daily/by day), nocturnal (by night). The biannual/biennial pair decides itself: -ennial counts years, -annual counts per year.

**That-which-cannot-be set:** inevitable, incredible, invisible, inaudible, illegible, incorrigible, inexplicable — all 'in-/il- + verb of perception or action'. The stem names the verb ('read' → illegible), so link each to its verb: believe→incredible, see→invisible, hear→inaudible, read→illegible, avoid→inevitable, correct→incorrigible.

tricks.title: Ruler-first matching
tricks.body: Underline WHO rules in the stem (people, rich, officials, one, God) and match to democracy/plutocracy/bureaucracy/autocracy/theocracy. The stem hands you the answer's head word.

tricks.title: Verb-link the negatives
tricks.body: Chain each 'cannot-be' word to its verb: read→illegible, believe→incredible, see→invisible. Stems always quote the verb.

tricks.title: Dead-word precision
tricks.body: About the dead: praise → eulogy, mourning-poem → elegy, tomb-writing → epitaph. Three cards, three certain marks.

mistakes: Choosing 'astrology' for a scientific study of stars.
Swapping biannual (twice a year) and biennial (every two years).
Using 'elegy' where praise of the dead is asked (that is 'eulogy').
Confusing anarchy (no government) with autocracy (one ruler).
subtopics.notes:
### Government words: who rules?
Every government word answers one question: **who holds the power?** Find the ruler in the stem, then match it.

| Ruled by | Word |
|---|---|
| the people (through elected members) | democracy |
| one person with total power | autocracy / dictatorship |
| a king or queen | monarchy |
| the rich | plutocracy |
| nobles, the upper class | aristocracy |
| a small group | oligarchy |
| officials in government offices | bureaucracy |
| religious leaders, in God's name | theocracy |
| nobody (no government, no law) | anarchy |

Worked example: *Government by the wealthy* → pluto = wealth → **plutocracy**.

### Speech and writing words
These words about speaking and writing come in confusing pairs.
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| elegy | a sad poem mourning the dead |
| eulogy | a speech or writing praising someone (often after death) |
| epitaph | words written on a tomb |
| soliloquy | speaking one's thoughts aloud when alone (as in a play) |
| extempore | spoken without preparation |
| prologue / epilogue | opening part / closing part of a play or book |
| biography / autobiography | life story written by another / by oneself |
| anthology | a collection of poems or stories |

**The three 'dead' words:** mourning poem → elegy, praise → eulogy, tomb writing → epitaph. Learn them as a set of three.

### Time words
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| annual | once a year |
| biannual | twice a year |
| biennial | once in two years |
| perennial | lasting through the years |
| centenary | 100th anniversary |
| decade / century / millennium | 10 / 100 / 1000 years |
| nocturnal | active at night |
| diurnal | active in the daytime |

Memory tip: **-ennial** counts years (biennial = every 2 years); **-annual** counts times in a year (biannual = 2 times a year).

### 'That which cannot be ___' words
These start with *in-*, *il-* or *im-* (meaning 'not'). The verb in the stem gives the answer.
| Cannot be ... | Word |
|---|---|
| read (handwriting) | illegible |
| seen | invisible |
| heard | inaudible |
| believed | incredible |
| avoided | inevitable |
| conquered | invincible |
| corrected or reformed | incorrigible |
| wiped out or removed (a mark) | indelible |

Trap: **illegible** (cannot be read) vs **ineligible** (not qualified). They sound alike but mean totally different things.

### How to answer
1. Decide the type: government, speech/writing, time, or 'cannot be'.
2. Find the key word in the stem: the ruler, the kind of writing, the number of years, or the verb.
3. Match it, then check the look-alike pair.

### Quick revision
- Ruler decides: people → democracy, rich → plutocracy, officials → bureaucracy, God → theocracy, none → anarchy.
- Dead words: elegy (mourning), eulogy (praise), epitaph (tomb).
- Biannual = twice a year; biennial = every two years.
- Cannot-be: read → illegible, conquer → invincible, correct → incorrigible, avoid → inevitable.

patterns.name: Government or rule by ...
patterns.howToSpot: Stem: 'Government by ...', 'Rule by ...', or 'A state with no government'.
patterns.logic:
1. Underline the ruler (people, rich, officials, God, nobody).
2. Match to the -cracy or -archy word.
3. Reject words whose ruler differs.

*Why it works:* the first part of each word names the ruler.

example.q: *Government by a small group of powerful people* — (a) oligarchy (b) monarchy (c) democracy (d) anarchy
example.solution: oligo = few → **(a) oligarchy**.

patterns.name: Speech and literary words
patterns.howToSpot: Stem is about a poem, speech, tomb writing, life story or talking alone.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide what the writing does (mourns, praises, marks a tomb, tells a life).
2. Match: mourns → elegy, praises → eulogy, tomb → epitaph, own life → autobiography, alone → soliloquy.
3. Double-check the elegy/eulogy pair.

*Why it works:* the options are usually drawn from this small, confusing set.

example.q: *A collection of poems by different writers* — (a) anthology (b) biography (c) epilogue (d) elegy
example.solution: Collection → **(a) anthology**.

patterns.name: Time and frequency words
patterns.howToSpot: Stem mentions how often (every two years, twice a year) or when (at night, 100th anniversary).
patterns.logic:
1. Note the exact number and unit.
2. Apply the rule: -ennial counts years, -annual counts per year.
3. For day/night use diurnal/nocturnal.

*Why it works:* the options differ only in the counting, so precise reading wins.

example.q: *Happening twice a year* — (a) biannual (b) biennial (c) annual (d) perennial
example.solution: Twice a year → **(a) biannual**. Biennial is every two years.

patterns.name: 'That which cannot be ___' words
patterns.howToSpot: Stem: 'That which cannot be read / seen / conquered / corrected'.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the verb in the stem.
2. Recall the in-/il- word built on that verb.
3. Watch the sound-alike (illegible vs ineligible).

*Why it works:* each negative word is built on exactly one verb.

example.q: *That which cannot be heard* — (a) inaudible (b) invisible (c) illegible (d) indelible
example.solution: Heard → audio → **(a) inaudible**.

subtopics.title: Exam strategy for one-word substitution
subtopics.concept:
Tier 1 gives 1–2 OWS items; Tier 2 a few more. Like vocabulary, these are 15-second marks governed by recall — so the strategy is a *banking* strategy.

**Bank in categories, not lists.** One day: all -cide words. Next: fear words. Next: places. Categories cross-link (regicide joins reg- king with -cide killing), and cross-linked memories survive exam stress.

**Daily 10-minute rotation:** 10 new words + 20 old words read aloud. Weekend: 30-word mixed self-test. Every OWS word you meet in mocks goes into the personal sheet — repeats are frequent.

**In the exam:**
1. Read the stem and classify the family (killing? fear? study? person? place? group? government? cannot-be?).
2. Reject options from other families — usually two die here.
3. Match the stem's exact object (bees not birds; king not brother; praise not mourning).
4. If two options remain in-family, take the more specific one — OWS stems reward specificity (regicide beats homicide for 'murder of a king').

**Never leave it blank.** Even at 50-50 within a family, choose — no negative marking economics justify a skip on a recall item.

**Do not over-invest.** OWS is worth a couple of marks; the bank in this topic (150+ words) plus your mock sheet is sufficient. Beyond that, hours belong to RC and grammar.

tricks.title: Specificity rule
tricks.body: When two options fit the family, the stem's detail decides: 'brother' → fratricide, not homicide; 'twice a year' → biannual, not annual.

tricks.title: Stem-object underline
tricks.body: Underline the noun the word must carry (bees, grain, king, tomb). One underline removes half the options.

tricks.title: Mock-word ledger
tricks.body: Keep one running sheet titled 'OWS from mocks'. Most repeats come from your own past mistakes, not from unknown words.

mistakes: Reading the OWS bank once and expecting recall a month later.
Choosing a same-family but wrong-object word under time pressure.
Skipping the item when two options confuse, instead of applying specificity.
Spending entire revision days on OWS while grammar and RC — the real marks — wait.
subtopics.notes:
### Where one-word substitution fits
Most papers in SSC, Railway and Banking exams have one or two one-word-substitution questions. Each takes about 15 seconds if you know the word. It is a **memory topic**, so your plan should be about building and revising a word bank.

### Build the bank by category
Do not learn a random alphabetical list. Learn one category at a time:
1. Killing words (-cide) and fear words (-phobia).
2. Study words (-logy) and people words (jobs, habits).
3. Places and groups.
4. Government, speech, time and 'cannot be' words.
5. Medical words (anti-, epi-/pan-/endemic).
6. Direction and contrast pairs (emigrant/immigrant, introvert/extrovert, amateur/professional).

Words in one category support each other in memory. When you meet a new word in a mock test, add it to a **personal sheet** under its category.

### Daily 10-minute routine
- 10 new words + 20 old words, read aloud with the meaning.
- Every weekend: a 30-word mixed self-test.
- Any word you miss twice goes on a **weak list** that you revise every week.

### The four-step method in the exam
1. **Classify the stem:** killing? fear? study? person? place? group? government? medical?
2. **Remove other families:** options from a different family are usually wrong.
3. **Match the exact detail:** bees, not birds; mother, not father; whole world, not one area.
4. **Prefer the specific word:** if two options fit, choose the one that matches the stem's detail. For *killing of one's mother*, **matricide** beats the general *homicide*.

### Medical and science words
| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| antidote | medicine against a poison |
| antiseptic | substance applied to wounds to stop infection |
| anaesthetic | substance that removes the feeling of pain |
| antibiotic | medicine that kills bacteria inside the body |
| epidemic | disease spreading widely in one area at one time |
| pandemic | disease spreading over many countries or the whole world |
| endemic | disease always present in a particular area |
| convalescent | recovering after an illness |

### Direction and contrast pairs
| Pair | Difference |
|---|---|
| emigrant / immigrant | leaves his country / comes into a new country |
| introvert / extrovert | turned inward, shy / outgoing, sociable |
| amateur / professional | does it for pleasure / does it as a paid job |
| novice / veteran | beginner / very experienced |

### Spelling-based questions
Newer papers sometimes say *'Select the correctly spelt word that can substitute ...'*. All four options are the same word spelt differently. Know the word, then check its tricky letters: con-va-les-**cent**, athe-**ist**, obso-**lete**. Say the word in syllables and match each part.

### Never leave it blank?
If you have removed two options and are sure the answer is in the remaining two, choose using the specific-detail rule. If you have no idea at all, remember that most exams have negative marking — a blind guess is not wise.

### Quick revision
- Category-wise bank + personal sheet from mocks + weekly weak list.
- Four steps: classify → remove other families → match the detail → prefer the specific word.
- Medical: epidemic (one area), pandemic (world), endemic (always in an area).
- Pairs: emigrant/immigrant, introvert/extrovert, amateur/professional.
- Spelling items: break the word into syllables.

patterns.name: Specific word beats the general word
patterns.howToSpot: Two options fit the family; one is general (homicide, epidemic) and one matches the stem's exact detail (matricide, pandemic).
patterns.logic:
1. Underline the exact detail in the stem (mother, whole world, new to the job).
2. Test each in-family option against that detail.
3. Pick the one that matches it exactly.

*Why it works:* one-word substitution always wants the most precise single word.

example.q: *The killing of a human being by another* — (a) homicide (b) genocide (c) suicide (d) regicide
example.solution: No special victim is named, only 'a human being' → **(a) homicide**.

patterns.name: Medical and science words
patterns.howToSpot: Stem is about a medicine, a disease's spread, or recovery.
patterns.logic:
1. Decide the job: against poison, against germs on a wound, removes pain, kills bacteria inside.
2. For diseases decide the spread: one area now (epidemic), world (pandemic), always in one area (endemic).
3. Match and check the anti- look-alikes.

*Why it works:* the anti- and -demic words differ by one precise idea.

example.q: *A medicine that kills bacteria inside the body* — (a) antibiotic (b) antidote (c) antiseptic (d) anaesthetic
example.solution: Kills bacteria, taken into the body → **(a) antibiotic**.

patterns.name: Correctly spelt one-word substitute
patterns.howToSpot: Stem says 'Select the correctly spelt word ...'; all four options are one word in different spellings.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the word from the meaning.
2. Break it into syllables and check each part.
3. Watch common slips: -ent/-ant, -ie-/-ei-, single/double letters.

*Why it works:* only one spelling is standard; the rest differ in one tricky syllable.

example.q: Correctly spelt word for *a person who does not believe in God*: (a) atheist (b) athiest (c) atheest (d) aithiest
example.solution: athe + ist → **(a) atheist**.

patterns.name: Direction and contrast pairs
patterns.howToSpot: Options contain both members of a pair (emigrant/immigrant, introvert/extrovert, amateur/professional).
patterns.logic:
1. Find the direction or contrast in the stem (leaving or entering? inward or outward? pleasure or pay?).
2. Choose the matching member.
3. Use the prefix: e-/ex- = out, im-/in- = in.

*Why it works:* the prefix encodes the direction, so it decides the pair.

example.q: *A person who is outgoing and enjoys the company of others* — (a) extrovert (b) introvert (c) recluse (d) misanthrope
example.solution: extro = outward → **(a) extrovert**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem begins 'One who...' or 'A person who...' and names a job, habit or nature; all four options are person words.
pyqPatterns.approach: Underline the exact detail in the stem — the object of the job (maps, children, dictionary) or the habit (drinks, wastes money, easily fooled). Then match the option that owns exactly that detail, and reject the partner word (widow/widower, miser/spendthrift) planted among the options.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *One who eats too much*
example.solution: **Glutton**. Gullible (easily cheated) and spendthrift (wastes money) are other person words that describe different habits.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem says 'The killing of ...' and may or may not name a special victim (mother, brother, king, infant, race).
pyqPatterns.approach: Match the victim to its root: mater = mother, pater = father, frater = brother, geno = race. If no special victim is named, the general word homicide is right. All four options are usually -cide words, so the victim decides.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *The killing of an infant*
example.solution: **Infanticide**. Genocide would need a whole race as the victim; homicide names no victim at all.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'An abnormal fear of ...' points to a -phobia word; 'The study of ...' or 'The science of ...' points to a -logy word.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix the family first (fear or study), then match the root to the thing feared or studied: hydro = water, acro = heights, ornitho = birds, entomo = insects, seismo = earthquakes. Watch the entomology/etymology twin.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *The study of birds*
example.solution: **Ornithology**. Entomology is insects — one letter group apart, which is exactly the confusion the examiner tests.

pyqPatterns.pattern: A place where ... / A group of ...
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem names a stored thing or resident ('A place where bees are kept') or a collection ('A group of wolves').
pyqPatterns.approach: Find the key noun and recall its fixed partner: bees → apiary, grain → granary, coins → mint, monks → monastery, wolves → pack, lions → pride, islands → archipelago. Check the one-letter traps (apiary/aviary) and the partner-place traps (monastery/convent) before marking.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *A place where birds are kept*
example.solution: **Aviary**. Apiary (bees) differs by one letter and is always planted beside it.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Government by ...' or 'Rule by ...' followed by the ruler — the people, the rich, officials, God, a king, nobody.
pyqPatterns.approach: Name the ruler in the stem and match it: people → democracy, rich → plutocracy, officials → bureaucracy, God → theocracy, one person → autocracy, a few → oligarchy, none → anarchy. The first part of each word names the ruler.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *Government by officials*
example.solution: **Bureaucracy**. The ruler here is the office machinery, not the people (democracy) or the rich (plutocracy).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem is about a poem, speech, tomb writing, life story, or about how often something happens.
pyqPatterns.approach: Decide what the writing does (mourns → elegy, praises → eulogy, marks a tomb → epitaph, own life → autobiography). For frequency apply the counting rule: -ennial counts years (biennial = every two years), -annual counts times per year (biannual = twice a year).

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *A speech praising a person who has died*
example.solution: **Eulogy**. It praises; an elegy mourns. The two are always planted together.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem is about a medicine (against poison, germs, pain) or about a disease's spread (one area, the whole world, always present).
pyqPatterns.approach: For medicines, fix the job: against poison → antidote, kills bacteria inside → antibiotic, cleans wounds outside → antiseptic, removes feeling → anaesthetic. For diseases fix the spread: one area now → epidemic, the world → pandemic, always in one area → endemic.

example.q: Select the option that can substitute the given group of words: *A disease spreading rapidly in one area*
example.solution: **Epidemic**. Pandemic would need many countries; endemic is the constant-presence word, not rapid spread.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem says 'Select the correctly spelt word ...' and all four options are the same word in different spellings.
pyqPatterns.approach: Recall the word from the meaning, then break it into syllables and check each part against the options. Watch the classic slips: ie/ei order, -ent/-ant endings, single or double letters (convalescent, atheist, obsolete).

example.q: Correctly spelt word for *one who walks in his sleep*: somnambulist / somnambulyst / somnabulist / somnambulast
example.solution: **Somnambulist** — somn (sleep) + ambul (walk) + ist. Only the -ist ending and the u after ambul are correct.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Murder of a king
solvedExamples.solution: The stem is a killing word (-cide family). Within the family, the object decides: rex/reg = king → **regicide**. *Homicide* is killing of a human in general, *genocide* of a race, *infanticide* of an infant — all real words planted as family-mates.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Family first (-cide), then the root object (rex = king).

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where bees are kept
solvedExamples.solution: Place stems are anchored by the stored object: bees → **apiary**. *Aviary* is the one-letter neighbour (birds), *aquarium* holds fish, *granary* grain.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Stored-object anchor: bees → apiary. Watch the aviary trap.

solvedExamples.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A medicine that counteracts poison
solvedExamples.solution: The anti- options form the family; the function decides: counteracts poison → **antidote**. *Antibiotic* kills bacteria, *antiseptic* prevents infection on wounds, *anaesthetic* removes sensation.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Function matching within the anti- family.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who loves books
practice.solution: Biblio = book + phile = lover → **bibliophile**. *Philatelist* collects stamps, *lexicographer* compiles dictionaries, *philanthropist* loves humankind through charity.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A person who talks in his sleep
practice.solution: Somni = sleep + loqui = speak → **somniloquist**. *Somnambulist* walks in sleep (ambul = walk) — the classic sibling trap; *insomniac* cannot sleep at all.
practice.shortcut: somni- (sleep) + verb root decides: walk vs speak.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Government by the people through their elected representatives
practice.solution: Demos = people + cracy = rule → **democracy**. The stem names the ruler ('the people'); the other options name one ruler, officials, and nobles respectively.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who can use both hands with equal ease
practice.solution: Ambi = both + dextr = right hand/skill → **ambidextrous**. *Ambivalent* means having mixed feelings, *amphibious* means living on land and water — the ambi-/amphi- family tempts, the dextr root decides.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where bees are kept
practice.solution: Bees are kept in an **apiary**; *aviary* (one letter away) keeps birds, *aquarium* fish, *granary* grain.
practice.shortcut: Stored-object anchor; the aviary trap is deliberate.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The act of killing one's own brother
practice.solution: Frater = brother → **fratricide**. *Patricide* kills the father, *regicide* the king, *genocide* a whole community — all -cide family-mates separated by the relation root.
practice.shortcut: Family root decides the relation: frater = brother.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A speech delivered without any preparation
practice.solution: Unprepared speech = **extempore**. *Epilogue* closes a play, *monologue* is a long one-person speech (prepared or not), *elocution* is the art of clear speaking.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who studies the stars and other heavenly bodies scientifically
practice.solution: The word 'scientifically' fixes **astronomer** — the scientist of the sky. *Astrologer* predicts fates from star positions; *cosmonaut* travels; *geologist* studies the earth.
practice.shortcut: Science vs prediction: astronomer vs astrologer — the stem's adjective decides.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

An abnormal fear of enclosed spaces
practice.solution: Claustro = enclosed → **claustrophobia**. The family: hydro- water, acro- heights, xeno- foreigners — the stem names the feared object and the suffix names the family.
practice.shortcut: phobia family; match the feared object.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Words inscribed on a tomb
practice.solution: Tomb inscription = **epitaph**. *Epilogue* ends a play, *elegy* mourns in verse, *epigram* is a witty short saying — the epi- family is planted wholesale.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A person appointed to hear both sides and settle a dispute
practice.solution: An **arbitrator** is the authorised settler of disputes. *Agitator* stirs trouble, *dictator* rules absolutely, *philanthropist* gives to charity — different families entirely.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of lions
practice.solution: Lions live in a **pride**. *Herd* suits cattle, *swarm* bees, *flock* sheep or birds — the four collective options are swapped around in every paper.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who is present everywhere at the same time
practice.solution: Omni = all + present → **omnipresent**. The omni-triplet: -potent (power), -scient (knowledge), -present (place) — the stem names the dimension.
practice.shortcut: Omni- family: match the ending to the stem's dimension (place → present).

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A medicine that counteracts the effects of poison
practice.solution: Counteracts poison = **antidote**. *Antibiotic* attacks bacteria, *antiseptic* prevents wound infection, *anaesthetic* kills sensation during surgery.
practice.shortcut: anti- family; function match: poison → antidote.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

That which cannot be avoided
practice.solution: Cannot be avoided = **inevitable**. Link each option to its verb: conquer→invincible, see→invisible, believe→incredible. The stem's verb ('avoided') picks its partner.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The killing of one's own mother
practice.solution: mater = mother, so killing of the mother = **matricide**. Patricide is the father, fratricide the brother; no special victim is named in genocide.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The killing of a whole race or community
practice.solution: geno = race, so killing of a whole race = **genocide**. Homicide is a general killing of a human being; the stem names a race.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

An abnormal fear of heights
practice.solution: acro = height, so fear of heights = **acrophobia**. Hydrophobia is fear of water, xenophobia of foreigners, agoraphobia of open or crowded places.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

An abnormal fear of water
practice.solution: hydro = water, so fear of water = **hydrophobia**. Nyctophobia is fear of darkness, photophobia fear of light.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The scientific study of insects
practice.solution: entomo = insect, so the study of insects = **entomology**. Etymology (word origins) is the classic one-letter-group trap; ornithology is birds.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The scientific study of earthquakes
practice.solution: seismo = earthquake, so **seismology**. Archaeology studies the past by digging; anthropology studies humankind.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The practice of having more than one spouse at the same time
practice.solution: poly = many + gamy = marriage → **polygamy**. Monogamy is one spouse; misogamy is hatred of marriage, misogyny hatred of women.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who collects stamps as a hobby
practice.solution: A stamp collector = **philatelist**. A numismatist collects coins; a bibliophile loves books; a philanderer is a man who flirts.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who draws maps
practice.solution: Maps → **cartographer**. The -grapher options are job words for other objects: beautiful writing, dance movements and films.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A doctor who treats diseases of children
practice.solution: Children → **paediatrician**. The others treat skin, heart and the mind.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who compiles a dictionary
practice.solution: lexicon = dictionary, so its maker is a **lexicographer**. A demographer studies population statistics.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who never drinks alcohol
practice.solution: Total abstainer from alcohol = **teetotaller**. A glutton overeats; a spendthrift wastes money; an ascetic lives a strict simple life, which is broader than abstaining from drink.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who is easily cheated or deceived
practice.solution: One who believes too readily and is easily fooled = **gullible**. A sceptic doubts everything — almost the opposite; a cynic expects selfish motives; a pessimist expects the worst.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A woman whose husband has died
practice.solution: The man who has lost his wife is a widower; the woman is a **widow**. The pair word is the planted trap.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who spends money wastefully
practice.solution: Wasteful spender = **spendthrift**. A miser saves excessively and hates spending — the opposite partner; a hoarder piles things up; a steward manages another's household.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who can speak many languages
practice.solution: poly = many + glot = tongue → **polyglot**. A polymath knows many subjects, not languages; a monoglot speaks only one — the planted opposite.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who hates women
practice.solution: mis = hate + gyn = woman → **misogynist**. A misanthrope hates mankind in general; a misogamist hates marriage.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where grain is stored
practice.solution: Grain → **granary**. Aviary is for birds, apiary for bees, arsenal for weapons — all stored-thing places for other things.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where aircraft are kept and repaired
practice.solution: Aircraft → **hangar**. 'Hanger' (one who/that which hangs clothes) is the spelling trap; a dockyard serves ships.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where weapons and ammunition are stored
practice.solution: Weapons → **arsenal**. A mortuary keeps dead bodies; a mint makes coins.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where monks live as a community
practice.solution: Monks (men) → **monastery**; nuns (women) → convent. A seminary trains priests; an orphanage houses orphans.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where coins are manufactured
practice.solution: Coins are made at a **mint**. A treasury keeps public money but does not make coins; a refinery processes oil or ore.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A place where stars and planets are studied with telescopes
practice.solution: Stars studied through telescopes → **observatory**. A planetarium is a domed hall that shows an artificial sky; it is not a study place.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A large group of bees flying together
practice.solution: Bees → **swarm**. Flock is for sheep or birds, herd for cattle, pack for wolves or dogs.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of wolves
practice.solution: Wolves hunt in a **pack**. Lions take pride, cattle take herd, bees swarm.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of stars forming a fixed pattern
practice.solution: A fixed pattern of stars = a **constellation** (like the Great Bear). A galaxy is a vast system of millions of stars, not a named pattern.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of ships sailing together
practice.solution: Ships → **fleet**. Flock is for birds or sheep; a bouquet is a bunch of flowers.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A group of islands lying close together
practice.solution: A cluster of islands = **archipelago**. A peninsula is land almost surrounded by water — the planted geography look-alike.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Government by the rich
practice.solution: pluto = wealth → rule by the rich = **plutocracy**. Democracy is rule by the people, autocracy by one person, bureaucracy by officials.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Government by religious leaders who claim to rule in the name of God
practice.solution: theo = God → **theocracy**. Monarchy is rule by a king; anarchy is the absence of any rule.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A state of society with no government and no law
practice.solution: an = without + archy = rule → **anarchy**, lawlessness. Oligarchy is rule by a few; autonomy is self-rule of a region within a state.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A poem of mourning for the dead
practice.solution: A sad poem mourning the dead = **elegy**. A eulogy is a speech or writing that praises the dead — mourns vs praises is the trap.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The story of a person's life written by the person himself
practice.solution: auto = self → written by oneself = **autobiography**. A biography is written by another person; an anthology is a collection of poems or stories; an almanac is a yearly book of dates and facts.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Happening once in two years
practice.solution: The -ennial family counts years: once in two years = **biennial**. Biannual means twice in one year — the classic trap.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Animals that remain active at night
practice.solution: Active at night = **nocturnal** (owl, bat). Diurnal animals are active by day; aquatic live in water; arboreal live in trees.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

Handwriting that cannot be read
practice.solution: Cannot be read = **illegible**. Ineligible means not qualified — the sound-alike trap; illiterate means unable to read or write; inaudible cannot be heard.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

That which cannot be conquered or defeated
practice.solution: vinc = conquer (as in victory) → cannot be conquered = **invincible**. Invisible cannot be seen; inevitable cannot be avoided; incorrigible cannot be corrected.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

The killing of one human being by another
practice.solution: No special victim is named, only 'a human being' (homi = man), so the general word **homicide** is right. The stem is not about a race, king or oneself.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A disease that spreads over many countries and the whole world
practice.solution: pan = all → world-wide spread = **pandemic**. An epidemic spreads fast but stays within one area; endemic is always present in one area; quarantine is a period of isolation, not a disease word.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A child whose parents are dead
practice.solution: The exact single word is **orphan**. 'Bereaved' only means having lost someone — the general word the specific-word rule beats; a widow lost a husband; a hermit lives alone by choice.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A medicine that destroys bacteria inside the body
practice.solution: **Antibiotics** are taken to kill bacteria within. An antidote works against a poison, an antiseptic cleans wounds from outside, an anaesthetic removes the feeling of pain.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A disease that is always present in a particular area or among a particular people
practice.solution: en = in → always present within one area = **endemic**. Epidemic and pandemic describe sudden spread, not constant presence; contagious means spreading by contact.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A drug that takes away the feeling of pain during an operation
practice.solution: an = without + aisthesis = feeling → **anaesthetic** removes sensation. The other anti- words fight germs or poison, not pain.

practice.q:
Select the correctly spelt word that can substitute the given group of words.

A person who does not believe in the existence of God
practice.solution: The correct spelling is **atheist**: athe + ist. The other options swap the ie/ei letters or distort the syllables.

practice.q:
Select the correctly spelt word that can substitute the given group of words.

One who is recovering health after an illness
practice.solution: **Convalescent** — say it in syllables: con-va-les-cent. The ending is -escent, and the third syllable keeps the s before c.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

A person who is outgoing and mixes freely with others
practice.solution: extro = outward → interested in what is outside = **extrovert**. An introvert is turned inward; a recluse and a misanthrope avoid people altogether.

practice.q:
Select the option that can substitute the given group of words.

One who comes into a foreign country to live there permanently
practice.solution: im/in = in → one who comes IN = **immigrant**. An emigrant leaves his own country (e-/ex- = out); the same person is an emigrant there and an immigrant here.
